title: A History of Eighteenth Century Literature
description: Published in 1889 and the standard Victorian history of eighteenth-century English literature: a survey from Dryden to the Romantics, written for the general reader.
plot_or_argument: Gosse traces the poetry, drama, prose and criticism of the age in a continuous narrative, with chapters on Pope, Swift, Addison, Johnson, Gray, Goldsmith, Cowper and the novelists, and gives the century a coherent literary shape.
historical_context: The 1880s, the growth of English studies in the universities, and the demand for a national literary history.
literary_significance: Gosse's history was the standard account of eighteenth-century English literature for a generation and helped to establish the academic study of the period; it is a key document in the making of the English literary canon.

title: Henrik Ibsen
description: Published in 1907 and Gosse's life of the Norwegian dramatist whose work he had done more than anyone to introduce to England.
plot_or_argument: Gosse follows Ibsen from the poverty of Skien and Grimstad through the years in Rome and Munich to the social dramas and the late symbolic plays, and gives an account of the English reception of each.
historical_context: The 1880s-1900s, the English production of Ibsen, the censorship of the Lord Chamberlain, and the New Drama movement.
literary_significance: Gosse's Ibsen is the book through which the English literary world understood the dramatist, and Gosse himself was the decisive agent in the English reception of modern European drama; the volume is a central document of the making of the modern English theatre.

title: Life of Algernon Charles Swinburne
description: Published in 1917 and the authorised life of the poet by his friend and executor: the standard early biography of Swinburne and a remarkable portrait of the Victorian literary world.
plot_or_argument: Gosse traces Swinburne's Northumberland childhood, Eton and Oxford, the friendship with Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelites, the scandal of Poems and Ballads, the years at Holmwood with Watts-Dunton, and the late Tory and De Profundis poems.
historical_context: The 1910s, the first generation of Victorian biography after the deaths of the principals, and the suppression of Swinburne's letters.
literary_significance: Gosse's Swinburne is a major Victorian biography and a primary source for the literary history of the 1860s; its omissions and suppressions have made it a case study in the ethics of literary biography.

title: The Blue Fairy Book
description: Published in 1889 and the first of the twelve 'coloured' fairy books: the volume that gave English children the classic French, German, Norwegian and English tales in a single collection.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Bronze Ring', 'East of the Sun and West of the Moon', 'The Yellow Dwarf', 'Little Red Riding-Hood', 'Cinderella', 'Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp', 'The Forty Thieves', 'Beauty and the Beast' and 'The Master Maid', among thirty-seven tales.
literary_form: Fairy-tale anthology (with illustrations by H. J. Ford and G. P. Jacomb-Hood)
historical_context: The 1880s, the Victorian fairy-tale revival, the folklore scholarship of the Folklore Society, and the golden age of the illustrated gift book.
literary_significance: The Blue Fairy Book created the modern English canon of the fairy tale and was the most important single agency in transmitting the world's folklore to English-speaking children; the twelve books together form the largest fairy-tale collection in the language.

title: Custom and Myth
description: Published in 1884 and Lang's most influential book of scholarship: essays arguing that myths and customs are survivals of an early stage of human thought, and that they can be studied comparatively across cultures.
plot_or_argument: Lang examines the myth of Cronus, the 'cattle-stealing' myth, the 'myth of the pouch', the Australian and Melanesian parallels to Greek myth, and argues against the solar-myth school of Max Müller that myths are survivals of savage thought rather than corrupted nature-worship.
historical_context: The 1880s, the new anthropology of Tylor and Frazer, the Folklore Society, and the comparative study of religion.
literary_significance: Custom and Myth is a founding text of the anthropological study of myth and of the theory of survivals; it changed the study of classical mythology and made folklore a serious academic subject in England.

title: The Iliad of Homer, Done into English Prose
description: Published in 1879 and the most widely read English translation of the Iliad of the Victorian period: a plain prose version designed to give the modern reader the effect of the original.
plot_or_argument: The translation follows the Iliad from the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon through the death of Patroclus and the return of Hector's body, in a prose that deliberately avoids the poetic diction of Pope and the archaism of Chapman.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian debate on Homer (Arnold versus Newman), and the growth of the Greek curriculum in the public schools.
literary_significance: Butcher and Lang's Iliad was the standard English Homer for a generation and a landmark in the theory of translation: its plain prose established the modern principle that Homer should be rendered in the language of the reader rather than in a pseudo-classical diction.

title: Letters to Dead Authors
description: Published in 1886 and Lang's most charming book of criticism: letters addressed to dead writers — Herodotus, Theocritus, Pope, Scott, Thackeray, Dickens, Poe, Stevenson — in which the critic talks to his masters.
plot_or_argument: Each letter is a short critical essay in the form of a personal address, mixing praise, complaint about modern misreadings, jokes about the writer's biographers, and exact quotation from the work.
historical_context: The 1880s, the essay tradition of Lamb and Hazlitt, the new professional literary journalism, and the Victorian cult of the writer's personality.
literary_significance: Letters to Dead Authors is the finest Victorian example of the personal critical essay and one of the books through which the Victorian reader's relation to the literary past was formed.

title: Poems (1893)
description: Published in 1893 with a preface by Francis Thompson and the volume that made Meynell's reputation: the collected shorter poems, including 'The Shepherdess', 'Renouncement', 'Parted', 'A Letter from a Girl to Her Own Old Age' and 'The Modern Poet'.
plot_or_argument: The poems range from the early 'Preludes' of 1875 to the religious lyrics of the 1890s; their subjects are the passing of time, the death of children, the discipline of renunciation and the sacramental presence of God in ordinary things.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Catholic revival, the new interest in the religious lyric, and the friendship of Francis Thompson and Coventry Patmore.
literary_significance: Meynell's Poems is the finest single volume of English Catholic lyric between Crashaw and the twentieth century; 'Renouncement' and 'The Shepherdess' are among the most anthologised poems in English, and her example made a place for a poetry of religious restraint in the age of Swinburne.

title: The Rhythm of Life and Other Essays
description: Published in 1893 and Meynell's first collection of essays: short meditations on time, childhood, poverty, art and the rhythm of the spiritual life.
plot_or_argument: The essays take a small subject — a clock, a child's sleep, a beggar at the door, the colour of the sky — and turn it into a meditation on time and eternity; 'The Rhythm of Life' itself argues that the spiritual life has a tempo that the modern world destroys.
historical_context: The 1890s, the English essay tradition, the Catholic revival, and the aesthetic appreciation of the ordinary.
literary_significance: The Rhythm of Life is one of the finest collections of English essays of the century and established Meynell as the successor of Lamb and Hazlitt in the meditative essay; her prose was admired by Ruskin, Meredith and Wilde.

title: The Spirit of Place and Other Essays
description: Published in 1899 and the second of Meynell's essay collections: studies of landscape, travel and the genius of particular places, from the English downs to Rome.
plot_or_argument: The essays consider what makes a place speak — the spirit of a river, the atmosphere of a town, the look of a country in a particular light — and argue that the artist's task is to see the place as it is rather than to impose a mood upon it.
historical_context: The 1890s, the vogue for the topographical essay, the English countryside movement, and the Catholic imagination of place.
literary_significance: The Spirit of Place is the classic English collection of topographical essays and a key text in the literature of place; it is the book in which Meynell's prose style reaches its greatest refinement.

title: Later Poems
description: Published in 1901 and the second collection of Meynell's verse: the poems of motherhood, infancy and bereavement that followed the deaths of two of her children.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Child', 'The Unknown God', 'Maternity', 'The Two Poets' and 'In Portugal', and its central subject is the loss of a child and the refusal of consolation that is not true.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian poetry of infancy after Patmore, and Meynell's own bereavements of 1888 and 1890.
literary_significance: Later Poems contains the finest English poems of infant death and maternal grief of the later nineteenth century; they are a permanent contribution to the poetry of bereavement, and their restraint makes them more powerful than the conventions of Victorian elegy allowed.

title: Reuben Sachs: A Sketch
description: Published in 1888 and the first sustained English novel of Anglo-Jewish middle-class life: a satire of a prosperous London Jewish family and the love story of a clever woman and an ambitious politician.
plot_or_argument: Judith Quixano, educated and passionate, loves Reuben Sachs, a rising Conservative politician determined to marry money and position; the family's marriage market and the pressures of the community defeat them both, and the novel ends with Reuben's engagement to a rich heiress and Judith's retreat into illness and faith.
principal_characters: Judith Quixano; Reuben Sachs; Leopold Leuniger; Esther Sachs; Rose Quixano; Bertie Lee-Harrison; the Cohen family
historical_context: The 1880s, the Anglo-Jewish gentry of Bayswater and Maida Vale, the debate on assimilation, and the first wave of Jewish immigration from eastern Europe.
literary_significance: Reuben Sachs is a landmark of English-Jewish literature: the first English novel to describe the Anglo-Jewish middle class from inside, and one of the first to analyse the position of the Jewish woman between community and modernity. Its reception — condemned by the Jewish press as a betrayal — is itself a chapter in the history of English Jewish identity.

title: The Romance of a Shop
description: Published in 1888 and the first English novel about women running a business in the age of the New Woman: four orphaned sisters open a photographic studio in Baker Street.
plot_or_argument: The Lorimer sisters, left penniless, set up as photographers; Fanny marries, Gertrude runs the studio, Lucy falls ill, and Phyllis is courted by the aesthete Lord Watergate; the novel ends with the studio closed and the sisters dispersed into marriage and work.
historical_context: The 1880s, the first generation of professional women, the new photography trade, and the debate on women's work.
literary_significance: The Romance of a Shop is the founding English novel of the woman's small business and one of the first to treat women's professional work as a subject rather than a problem; its picture of the 1880s London of shops, studios and lodgings is a key document of the New Woman's world.

title: A Minor Poet and Other Verse
description: Published in 1884 and Levy's second collection: dramatic monologues spoken by the marginal and the defeated — a minor poet, a magician, a fallen woman, a suicide.
plot_or_argument: The title poem is the monologue of a poet who has failed and is about to die; the volume also contains 'Xantippe' (spoken by Socrates' wife), 'A Greek Girl', 'Christopher Found' and the elegiac lyrics of the city.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Browning vogue for the dramatic monologue, the woman's poetry of the 1880s, and the London literary world.
literary_significance: A Minor Poet is the finest English collection of dramatic monologues by a woman of the century: Levy takes the Browningesque form and turns it to the voices of the excluded, and the title poem is a classic statement of the artist's failure.

title: A London Plane-Tree and Other Verse
description: Published in 1889, the year of her death, and Levy's last collection: urban lyrics of London, the British Museum, the omnibus, the Thames and the plane trees.
plot_or_argument: The poems include 'A London Plane-Tree', 'Ballade of an Omnibus', 'The Street' and 'A March Day in London', and move between the city's anonymity and the wistfulness of the observer who loves it.
historical_context: The 1880s, the London poetry of the 1890s, the aesthetic interest in the city, and the vogue for the French forms of the ballade.
literary_significance: A London Plane-Tree is one of the founding collections of English urban poetry: Levy's London is the modern city of strangers, and her city poems prepared the way for the 1890s poetry of Davidson, Symons and Johnson.

title: The Ascent of Man
description: Published in 1889 and the most ambitious English poem of evolutionary ideas: a blank-verse epic of the ascent of humanity from the primeval slime to the socialist future.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves through the formation of the earth, the emergence of life, the age of the reptiles and mammals, the coming of man, the rise of religion and art, and ends with a vision of a future of human solidarity in which 'the Many' inherit the earth.
historical_context: The 1880s, Darwinism, the popular evolutionary epic of the period, and the socialist revival of the 1880s.
literary_significance: The Ascent of Man is the only Victorian evolutionary epic written by a woman and one of the most ambitious poems of the century: it brings together Darwin, Shelley and the socialist future in a way no other English poet attempted.

title: George Eliot
description: Published in 1883 in John Ingram's Eminent Women Series and the first full biography of George Eliot: a critical life written within three years of the novelist's death.
plot_or_argument: Blind follows Eliot from the Warwickshire childhood through the translation of Strauss and Feuerbach, the editorship of the Westminster Review, the union with Lewes, the novels and the late marriage, and gives careful readings of each of the major works.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Eminent Women Series, the new market for literary biography, and the debate on Eliot's private life.
literary_significance: Blind's George Eliot is a founding work of English feminist literary biography: it was the first attempt to take Eliot as a woman writer seriously and the first substantial critical account of the novels after her death.

title: Birds of Passage: Songs of the Orient and Occident
description: Published in 1895 and Blind's last collection: songs of travel and of the meeting of East and West, written after her journeys to Italy, Egypt and the Continent.
plot_or_argument: The poems move between the English landscape and the Mediterranean world, and include songs of the Bedouin, the Nile and the Italian cities as well as lyrics of love and death.
historical_context: The 1890s, the vogue for the Oriental lyric, the English traveller in Egypt, and the poetry of the 'world literature' movement.
literary_significance: Birds of Passage is a significant late-Victorian collection of comparative poetry and one of the few English volumes of the period to attempt a genuinely international lyric.

title: 'A Castaway'
description: Published in the collection Portraits in 1870 and the greatest Victorian poem spoken by a prostitute: the monologue of a woman of the town who has become rich and respectable and finds her life hollow.
plot_or_argument: The speaker addresses her maid and her own mirror, recalling her mother, her first seducer, her years of professional life and the loneliness of her present comfort, and refuses the sentimental alternatives of repentance or death.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Contagious Diseases Acts, the double standard, and the debate over the 'social evil'.
literary_significance: 'A Castaway' is the most important Victorian poem about prostitution and one of the finest dramatic monologues of the century: it gives the woman her own voice and refuses both the sentimental and the punitive ending, and it is a central text of Victorian feminist poetry.

title: Medea of Euripides
description: Published in 1878 and the standard Victorian English translation of Euripides's Medea: a version in blank verse that made the Greek tragedy a modern play about marriage and revenge.
plot_or_argument: Medea, betrayed by Jason, takes her revenge by killing his new bride and her own children, and escapes in the chariot of the sun; Webster's version emphasises the legal position of the foreign wife and the cold logic of the revenge.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian Greek revival, the position of the married woman under English law, and the debate on divorce.
literary_significance: Webster's Medea is the finest Victorian translation of a Greek tragedy and the one that made Medea a central text for the feminist reading of classical drama; it remains one of the standard English versions.

title: Portraits
description: Published in 1870 and the collection that established Webster as the leading woman poet of the dramatic monologue: studies of women's lives in their own voices.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'A Castaway', 'Medea in Athens', 'Circe', 'The Happiest Girl in the World', 'A Sister' and 'By the Sea', each a portrait of a woman at a moment of crisis.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Browning vogue, the woman's poetry of the 1860s-70s, and the debate on the 'woman question'.
literary_significance: Portraits is the central English collection of woman's dramatic monologues and one of the most important volumes of Victorian women's poetry; its range — from the classical witch to the London prostitute — is unmatched in the period.

title: Mother and Daughter: An Uncompleted Sonnet Sequence
description: Published after her death in 1895: an unfinished sonnet sequence on the relation of a mother and a daughter, and the last thing Webster wrote.
plot_or_argument: The sequence follows the daughter from infancy through childhood to the threshold of adult life, and the mother's apprehension of loss, change and the approach of her own death.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian sonnet revival, the poetry of family life, and the mother-daughter relation in Victorian writing.
literary_significance: Mother and Daughter is one of the first sustained English poems on the mother-daughter bond and a landmark of Victorian women's poetry; its unfinished state has made it a text of particular interest to modern criticism.

title: The Angel in the House
description: Published in four instalments between 1854 and 1862 and the most popular long poem of the Victorian age: the courtship and marriage of Felix Vaughan and Honoria Churchill, and the idealisation of the wife as the moral centre of the home.
plot_or_argument: Felix, a young poet, courts Honoria through a long sequence of domestic scenes, wins her, and the poem follows the marriage through its trials; the second half follows the widowed Felix and his second marriage to Jane, and ends with the death of Honoria and the transfiguration of married love.
literary_form: Long narrative poem in four parts (The Betrothal 1854, The Espousals 1856, Faithful for Ever 1860, The Victories of Love 1862)
meter_and_prosody: Mostly octosyllabic couplets in a plain, conversational narrative style, with lyric interludes.
historical_context: The 1850s, the ideal of the companionate marriage, the Oxford Movement, and the Victorian cult of domesticity.
literary_significance: The Angel in the House gave the Victorian age its name for the ideal wife and is the central poem of Victorian domestic ideology: it is the text against which the whole feminist critique of Victorian marriage was written, and its idealisation of the wife is still the standard image of the Victorian home.

title: The Unknown Eros and Other Odes
description: Published in 1877 and Patmore's greatest poetry: a series of odes on divine love, death and the mystical union of the soul with God, written after his conversion to Rome.
plot_or_argument: The odes move from 'Eros' and 'Psyche' through 'The Toys', 'The Azalea', 'Departure' and 'The Unknown Eros' to 'Amelia' and the vision of the love of God; their subject is the continuity of human love and divine love.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Catholic mystical tradition, the Swedenborgian and Dantean background, and Patmore's own bereavement and conversion.
literary_significance: The Unknown Eros is a landmark of English religious poetry and one of the strangest books of the nineteenth century: its long, unrhymed, free-breathing odes anticipated the rhythms of Hopkins and of modern free verse, and its mystical eroticism is unique in Victorian poetry.

title: The Victories of Love
description: Published in 1862 and the final part of The Angel in the House: the story of Felix Vaughan's second marriage to Jane, told through a series of verse letters, and of the death of Honoria.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the widowed Felix, his engagement to Jane, the marriage, the birth of their child and the death of Jane, and ends with a vision of the union of the lovers in heaven.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Victorian poetry of marriage and death, and the Tractarian theology of the resurrection of the body.
literary_significance: The Victories of Love completes the great Victorian poem of marriage and makes the case for the ordinary married life as a form of spiritual heroism; it is the source of the phrase 'the angel in the house' as a domestic ideal and of much of the later critique of it.
